title: Look for the Helpers: M. Camus, Meet Mr. Rogers
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Harriett Janetos frames the loneliness of teaching beginning reading through Fred Rogers's advice to look for the helpers, then builds her own instructional reading guide around exactly that idea: a curated set of golden-sentence quotations from researchers and practitioners across six chapters covering vocabulary, spelling, phonics, orthographic mapping, comprehension, and writing-to-read connections. She argues that even without strong institutional support, teachers can assemble a personal network of expert helpers through books, podcasts, and Substack, and she models this by pulling forward specific findings, such as invented spelling facilitating rather than hampering literacy development, and writing-about-text enhancing comprehension. The piece closes by reaching for Camus's Myth of Sisyphus, reframing the exhausting, repetitive labor of literacy instruction as a struggle that can still fill a teacher's heart, concluding that one must imagine teachers happy the way Camus imagined Sisyphus happy.
points: Curates specific research-backed 'golden sentences' across six literacy domains, including a finding that invented spelling facilitates rather than hampers early reading and spelling development.
Cites writing-to-read research (Graham and Hebert) showing that having students write about a text they are reading measurably enhances their comprehension of it.
Reframes the isolation of teaching beginning reading, which she calls 'the hardest job of all,' through Camus's Myth of Sisyphus, arguing the struggle itself can fill a teacher's heart.
Models a concrete solution to under-resourced schools: building a personal network of research 'helpers' through books, podcasts, webinars, and Substack rather than waiting on institutional support.
quotes: When I was a boy and I would see scary things in the news, my mother would say to me, look for the helpers, you will always find people who are helping.
Allowing children to engage in the analytical process of invented spelling, followed by appropriate feedback, has been found to facilitate learning to read and spell, not hamper the process.
The evidence is clear: writing can be a vehicle for improving reading. In particular, having students write about a text they are reading enhances how well they comprehend it.
To state the obvious, the reason why teachers need help is because teaching is hard, and teaching beginning reading efficiently and effectively may be the hardest job of all.

The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man's heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy. Is the struggle itself enough to fill a person's heart? You bet it is! One must imagine teachers happy.
